claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is initially in a solidified solid-solution state.
Temperature and strain rate are the proposed independent variables.
Changes in temperature and strain rate affect dislocation density in the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy.
Precipitation is an active structural mediator during testing of the solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy.
A dislocation-density-based crystal-plasticity model can describe microscale deformation and high-strain-rate behavior.
Precipitation strengthening contributes to strength and post-yield hardening in high-entropy alloys.
Solid-solution strengthening can increase yield strength in Co-free Fe-Mn-Ni-Cr alloys as Cr content increases.
The combined effects of dislocation evolution, precipitation strengthening, and solid-solution strengthening explain the temperature- and strain-rate-dependent behavior of Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The proposed mechanism produces an improved strength-ductility balance relative to the baseline alloy properties.
Increasing temperature and strain rate should improve the strength-ductility balance.
The mechanism is applicable over the temperature and strain-rate ranges used in testing.
The quantitative relationship among dislocation density, precipitation, and mechanical properties remains insufficiently understood.
Yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility measured at multiple temperatures and strain rates can be used to test the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The alloy is repeatedly specified as being in a solid-solution state, yet precipitation is treated as an active mediator without specifying that precipitates are present initially or form during testing. The same-system evidence reports sigma precipitation only after long exposures of 1000 h at 700 or 900 °C.

The hypothesis predicts improvement relative to a baseline defined only as the same alloy state, while the falsification rule introduces a directional prediction with simultaneously increasing temperature and strain rate. No reference temperature, reference strain rate, or separate controlled comparison is defined.
